text:
# Ambient occlusion (SSAO)

**Corners get darker.** Where a wall meets the floor, where crates are stacked,
under a ledge: real light does not reach in there, and a renderer without
ambient occlusion lights those creases exactly like the open ground beside
them. That is most of why a scene of plain boxes looks pasted together. One
attribute on `<tosi-b3d>` fixes it: `ssao="auto"`.

## Demo

Open the settings panel (the owl) and switch `ssao` between `off` and `on`. Watch the foot of
the walls, the gaps between the crates and the underside of the lintel, then
orbit in on the bust: a beard, a laurel and a collar are the kind of creased,
organic shape occlusion does most for. It works in VR too, with the default
`projected` method; `screen` is Babylon's own and switches itself off in a
headset. See "Two methods" below.

```js
import { b3d, b3dSun, b3dSkybox, b3dLight, b3dBox, b3dSphere, b3dGround, b3dProp, assetUrl, select3d, slider3d } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { tosi } from 'tosijs'

const { ssaoDemo } = tosi({ ssaoDemo: { mode: 'on', method: 'projected', strength: 1, radius: 2 } })

// A bust in faux alabaster: pale and semi-gloss, so occlusion is easy to see.
const bust = b3dProp({
  libraryUrl: assetUrl('tosijs-3d/ariosto-bust.glb'),
  meshName: 'Ariosto',
  scale: 0.8,
  x: 0.6, y: 1.4, z: -2.6, ry: 100,
})
function alabaster(babylon) {
  const mesh = bust.mesh ? bust.mesh.getChildMeshes()[0] : null
  if (mesh == null) return setTimeout(alabaster, 250, babylon)
  const material = new babylon.PBRMaterial('alabaster', mesh.getScene())
  material.albedoColor = new babylon.Color3(0.93, 0.9, 0.84)
  material.metallic = 0
  material.roughness = 0.4
  material.bumpTexture = mesh.material.bumpTexture
  mesh.material = material
}

const stone = '#b9b2a4'
const crate = '#a0764a'
preview.append(
  b3d(
    {
      ssao: ssaoDemo.mode,
      ssaoMethod: ssaoDemo.method,
      ssaoStrength: ssaoDemo.strength,
      ssaoRadius: ssaoDemo.radius,
      scenePanel: () => [
        select3d({ label: 'ssao', value: ssaoDemo.mode, options: ['off', 'auto', 'on'] }),
        select3d({ label: 'method', value: ssaoDemo.method, options: ['projected', 'screen'] }),
        slider3d({ label: 'strength', value: ssaoDemo.strength, min: 0, max: 3, step: 0.05 }),
        slider3d({ label: 'radius (m)', value: ssaoDemo.radius, min: 0.25, max: 6, step: 0.05 }),
      ],
      sceneCreated(el, BABYLON) {
        alabaster(BABYLON)
        const cam = el.scene.activeCamera
        // Target first: an orbit camera re-derives its position from the target.
        if (cam && cam.setTarget) cam.setTarget(new BABYLON.Vector3(-0.5, 1, 0.5))
        if (cam && cam.setPosition) cam.setPosition(new BABYLON.Vector3(6, 5, -10))
      },
    },
    b3dLight({ intensity: 0.9 }),
    b3dSun({ shadowTextureSize: 2048 }),
    b3dSkybox({ timeOfDay: 15 }),
    b3dGround({ size: 40, color: '#8f9a7a' }),
    // A corner of two walls, a doorway with a lintel, steps, stacked crates.
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'wall-a', width: 8, height: 3, depth: 0.5, x: 0, y: 1.5, z: 3, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'wall-b', width: 0.5, height: 3, depth: 6, x: -4.25, y: 1.5, z: 0.25, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'post-l', width: 0.5, height: 2.4, depth: 0.5, x: 2, y: 1.2, z: -1, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'post-r', width: 0.5, height: 2.4, depth: 0.5, x: 4, y: 1.2, z: -1, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'lintel', width: 3, height: 0.5, depth: 0.7, x: 3, y: 2.65, z: -1, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'step-1', width: 3, height: 0.25, depth: 1.5, x: -1.5, y: 0.125, z: 1.5, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'step-2', width: 3, height: 0.5, depth: 1, x: -1.5, y: 0.25, z: 2.1, color: stone }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'crate-1', size: 1, x: -3.2, y: 0.5, z: -0.5, color: crate }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'crate-2', size: 1, x: -2.1, y: 0.5, z: -0.3, ry: 12, color: crate }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'crate-3', size: 1, x: -2.7, y: 1.5, z: -0.4, ry: -8, color: crate }),
    b3dSphere({ meshName: 'ball', diameter: 1.2, x: 1, y: 0.6, z: 1.6, color: '#c8553d' }),
    b3dBox({ meshName: 'plinth', width: 0.6, height: 1, depth: 0.6, x: 0.6, y: 0.5, z: -2.6, color: stone }),
    bust
  )
)
```

## Two methods

`ssaoMethod` chooses how the occlusion is worked out. The default is
`projected`.

| `ssaoMethod` | Where it runs | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `projected` (default) | flat and in a headset | ours: see below |
| `screen` | flat only | Babylon's `SSAO2RenderingPipeline`, a post-process |

And `ssao` chooses whether it runs at all:

| `ssao` | |
| --- | --- |
| `off` (default) | off |
| `auto` | on if the device tier affords it (top tier only), and never in a headset |
| `on` | on, including in a headset when the method is `projected` |

## Projected

Occlusion is computed once, from a camera between the eyes, into a texture.
Every lit material then looks its own pixel up in that texture by world
position, the way cloud shadows and caustics do.

- It is correct in stereo, because each eye shades its own pixels and the
  darkening is attached to the surface.
- Nothing is post-processed, so the canvas keeps its antialiasing.
- It is not redrawn every frame. The lookup uses the matrix the texture was
  drawn with, so an old texture stays where it was in the world while the view
  moves. `ssaoRate` is redraws per second (default 30).
- The depth it works from is drawn by each mesh's own material, so skinned
  characters, instances and shader vertex animation (the crowd) are occluded
  in the pose you see.

What it costs is one extra pass over the opaque scene per redraw (depth only:
the materials skip their lighting), two small full-screen passes, and two
texture reads per lit pixel. On a Quest, in this demo, frame rate and CPU time
were the same with it on as off. That is a small scene. It has not been
measured on a heavy one, which is why `auto` stays off in a headset.

It concentrates its darkening in contacts and corners, where `screen` spreads
it more thinly. It is softer than `screen` on fine surface detail, because it
works from depth alone at reduced resolution and `screen` also reads each
material's normal map. A surface the middle camera could not see gets no
occlusion until the next redraw.

## Screen, and why it is flat only

`ssaoMethod="screen"` is Babylon's pipeline: it draws the opaque scene a second
time into a depth-and-normals buffer, samples that for every pixel, blurs the
result and composites it over the frame.

**It never runs in a headset.** A post-process chain on a WebXR camera does not
render per eye: it draws ONE image across both, on a Quest and in an emulated
headset alike, whether the chain is carried into the session or built inside
it. With this method occlusion is switched off before a session starts and back
on when it ends.

`ssao="always"` is a deprecated alias of `on`: it is accepted and warns once.

Sample count and resolution come from the device budget
(`PerfBudgets.ssaoSamples`, `ssaoRatio`), so you tune the LOOK and the tier
tunes the COST.

## Attributes (on `<tosi-b3d>`)

| Attribute | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ssao` | `'off'` | `off`, `auto` or `on`: see the tables above. LIVE |
| `ssaoStrength` | `1` | How dark a fully occluded crease gets. `0` is none. LIVE |
| `ssaoRadius` | `2` | How far, in metres, a surface looks for something occluding it. Small radii darken only tight creases; large ones shade whole alcoves. LIVE |
| `ssaoMethod` | `'projected'` | `projected` (flat and headset) or `screen` (Babylon's post-process, flat only). LIVE |
| `ssaoRate` | `30` | Projected only: redraws per second. `0` is every frame. LIVE |

## What is and is not occluded

Transparent meshes are left out of the depth-and-normals pass, so glass,
water seen through its alpha, particles and the cloud deck neither receive
nor cast occlusion. With `screen`, a mesh whose vertex shader moves its
vertices (the vertex-animated crowd) is occluded as if standing in its rest
pose; `projected` occludes it in the pose you see.

# gradient-filter

**A curve you can put a value through.** `PiecewiseLinearFilter` maps 0..1 to
0..1 through a list of control points, with straight lines between them.
Terrain uses one to reshape heights (a plateau, a terrace); see
[[slope-profile]] for the richer profiles built on the same idea, and
[[curve-field]] for the editable model.

```javascript
import { PiecewiseLinearFilter, plateauFilter } from 'tosijs-3d/gradient-filter'

const f = new PiecewiseLinearFilter([
  { x: 0, y: 0 },
  { x: 0.5, y: 0.1 }, // flat lowlands...
  { x: 1, y: 1 }, // ...then steep
])
f.evaluate(0.75) // 0.55

plateauFilter(4) // four flat steps
```

`identityFilter()` is the do-nothing curve.

text:
# Scene schemas

**JSON Schema for the scene primitives, so a consumer never hand-copies our
attributes.** No DOM, no Babylon — importable from a headless runner.

## Why this exists

A consumer that generates property panels from JSON Schema would otherwise write
one per component by hand: a copy of our attributes, maintained in another
repository, against a component it does not own. A copy like that drifts in both
directions — attributes that were never copied, defaults that disagree — and
nothing anywhere fails.

`lightSettingsSchema` does the same for a lamp: mark one field and the whole
lamp appears, with no schema on the consumer's side to maintain. This is that,
for the rest of the scene.

## These carry NO `x-widget`

Deliberately, and it is the one thing to get right. A widget token says "hand
this whole value to a custom editor" — correct for a light program, wrong here,
because a consumer's generated panel already renders numbers, colours, booleans
and enums perfectly well. Adding a token would point at an editor that does not
exist and break the panel that works.

What these DO carry is everything `initAttributes` cannot say: ranges, units,
enum members, colour formats, and which sliders want a log scale.

## `format`, not `x-widget`, is what a control keys off

`format: 'color'` is JSON Schema's own spelling, and it stays the one to read.
The dispatch a consumer wants is:

```javascript
// property.format === 'color'  →  a field that knows it holds a colour
ui.inputField({ value: current, type: 'color', handleChange })
// or the full picker
color3d({ value: current, handleChange })
```

`FieldType` has `'color'` for exactly this, so the two vocabularies line up:
a schema says `format`, a field says `type`, and neither has to guess. `x-widget`
stays reserved for values JSON Schema has no word for at all — a light program,
a curve — where the answer really is "hand the whole thing to a custom editor".

## The host has one too: `sceneSchemas.b3d`

`<tosi-b3d>` itself carries scene-level settings: the clear colour, glow, the
ambient occlusion look (`ssaoStrength`, `ssaoRadius`), the scene wind and the
time scale. `b3dSchema()` describes those and ONLY those. The host's other
attributes configure a viewer rather than a scene (camera limits, quality
tier, pixel ratio, gamepad and panel chrome, XR and pause behaviour) and are
declined by name in `SCENE_OMITTED.b3d`, so a document never stores someone's
laptop.

## Drift is a test, not a promise

The defaults here are duplicated from the components — there is no way to read
them without importing Babylon, which is exactly what makes this module usable.
So `scene-schemas.test.ts` imports the real components and fails if an attribute
is missing, extra, or disagrees on its default. The copy is allowed to exist
because it cannot silently rot.
title: Scene schemas

text:
# spatial-transform

Pure, dependency-free transform math for the **spatial attachment mechanics**
(see `SPATIAL-DESIGN.md`) — vector/quaternion ops plus the compose ↔ relative pair
that underpins *place-relative* and *transition* (re-parent preserving world pose).

Plain `{x,y,z}` / `{x,y,z,w}` objects, no Babylon, so it unit-tests headless like
[fly-by-wire](?fly-by-wire.ts). The Babylon
bridge (reading node world matrices, `setParent`, floating-origin world-root
flipping, the declarative elements) lives elsewhere and delegates the math here.

## Example — attach and re-attach

Capture a child's pose *relative* to a parent once, then recompose its world pose wherever the
parent goes — the math behind *place-relative* and *transition* (re-parent, keep the world pose):

```javascript
import { composePose, relativePose, quatFromAxisAngle } from 'tosijs-3d'

const table = { position: { x: 2, y: 0, z: 1 }, rotation: quatFromAxisAngle({ x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }, 0.5) }
const lamp = { position: { x: 2.3, y: 1, z: 1 }, rotation: { x: 0, y: 0, z: 0, w: 1 } }

const bolt = relativePose(table, lamp) // the lamp IN the table's frame — captured once
const moved = { position: { x: 8, y: 0, z: -4 }, rotation: quatFromAxisAngle({ x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }, 2.1) }
const lampNow = composePose(moved, bolt) // the lamp's new world pose after the table moved
```
title: spatial-transform

text:
# asset-url

A tiny indirection for referencing hosted blobs (models, textures, audio, …) by a
LOGICAL path, so demos/consumers aren't littered with a hostname and can retarget the
host in one place. `assetUrl('kenney/vehicles/car.glb')` resolves against a base set
once via `setAssetBase(...)`; the base defaults to empty, so paths resolve locally
(served from `static/`) for tests and offline dev. Already-absolute URLs
(`http(s)://`, `data:`, `blob:`) pass through untouched.

```javascript
import { setAssetBase, assetUrl, b3dLoader } from 'tosijs-3d'

setAssetBase('https://cdn.tosijs.net')          // once, e.g. in demo/site.ts
b3dLoader({ url: assetUrl('kenney/vehicles/car.glb') })
```

text:
# shadow-decal

A **soft blob shadow** — the oldest trick in real-time 3D, and still the right one in a lot of
places. Instead of routing a caster through the shadow map (expensive, and useless for anything
the cascaded map doesn't reach — a cloud at 140 m, a bird, a thrown grenade), you drop a dark,
soft-edged quad on the ground beneath it. It costs one textured, alpha-blended plane and no
shadow-map real estate at all.

It is deliberately NOT a real shadow: it doesn't know the caster's silhouette and it doesn't
sharpen with proximity. What it buys is *grounding* — the eye reads "this thing is above that
spot" — and for soft, high, or numerous casters (clouds, a flock, ambient debris) that reads
better than a crisp CSM shadow would anyway.

## Demo

**A floating crate, grounded by a soft blob.** No shadow map is involved — just one alpha quad
`createShadowDecal` drops on the ground beneath it. Drag to orbit; the decal reads the crate's
position over the floor.

```js
import { b3d, b3dBox, createShadowDecal } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { demoStage, orbitCam } from 'tosijs-3d/demo-utils'

const scene = b3d(
  {
    sceneCreated(el, BABYLON) {
      orbitCam(el, { radius: 15, beta: Math.PI / 3.2, target: [0, 1.2, 0] })
      // a soft grounding decal, placed where the SUN projects the floater onto the ground — so it
      // lines up with the light direction, not just straight down (which read wrong under an angled sun).
      const decal = createShadowDecal(el.scene, { size: 3.2 })
      const floater = new BABYLON.Vector3(0, 2.6, 0)
      const place = () => {
        const sun = el.scene.lights.find((l) => l.getClassName?.() === 'DirectionalLight')
        if (!sun) return
        const d = sun.direction.normalizeToNew() // light travel direction (points down-and-across)
        const t = floater.y / -d.y
        decal.position.set(floater.x + d.x * t, 0.02, floater.z + d.z * t)
        el.scene.onBeforeRenderObservable.removeCallback(place) // place once, then stop
      }
      el.scene.onBeforeRenderObservable.add(place)
    },
  },
  ...demoStage({ size: 24, tiles: 10, texture: '/tosi-warhol-testgrid.svg', timeOfDay: 10 }),
  // `_nocast` so no real CSM shadow competes with the decal — the decal IS the grounding shadow here
  b3dBox({ meshName: 'floater_nocast', size: 2, x: 0, y: 2.6, z: 0, color: '#c85a3a' }),
)
preview.append(scene)
```
```css
tosi-b3d { width: 100%; height: 100%; }
```

## Two ways to place one

- **`projectShadowDown`** — raycast straight down and lay the decal on whatever surface it hits
  (a character, a vehicle, a dropped item). Hugs terrain height; costs one ray per placement.
- **Flat placement** — just set `mesh.position`. For a *field* of decals (a whole cloud layer)
  a per-decal ray each frame is wasteful; sample the ground height once under the camera and
  drop every decal on that plane. Softness hides the lack of terrain-hugging.

## Sharing

All decals in a scene share **one** texture and **one** material (both cached per scene). Vary a
decal per-instance without breaking the sharing:

- **size** → `mesh.scaling.x/z`
- **darkness** → `mesh.visibility` (0…1, multiplies the blended alpha — works precisely because
  the material is shared and visibility is per-mesh)

That's the same discipline the clouds use for their blobs: one material, per-mesh transform and
visibility. See [b3d-clouds](?b3d-clouds.ts), the first consumer.

# demo-utils

**Scene-setup helpers for examples and prototypes** — the "when in doubt" defaults
that make a scene look like a scene instead of a test harness. Every live example
on this site uses them, which is why they are published: the code you copy off a
doc page should run in your project unchanged.

> ## ⚠️ These are DEV HELPERS. Do not build on them.
>
> They exist so examples run, and they are **not** covered by the care the main
> API gets:
>
> - **They can change or disappear in a patch release.** No deprecation period,
>   no migration note.
> - **They are tuned for looking good in a doc page**, not for your game — the
>   numbers are chosen to flatter a cube on a grey ground.
> - **They are not a design system.** `demoStage` is three components in a
>   trench coat; when you outgrow it, inline what it does and delete the import.
>
> Production code should compose `b3dSun`/`b3dSkybox`/`b3dGround` directly. If
> you find yourself wanting a helper to be *stable*, that is the signal it
> belongs in the main API — open an issue rather than pinning a version.

```js
import { b3d, b3dBox } from 'tosijs-3d'
import { demoStage, orbitCam } from 'tosijs-3d/demo-utils'

const scene = b3d(
  { sceneCreated: (el) => orbitCam(el, { radius: 8 }) },
  ...demoStage({ texture: '/tosi-warhol-testgrid.svg' }),
  b3dBox({ y: 1 }),
)
preview.append(scene)
```

## What's here

| Helper | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `demoStage(opts)` | Sun + fill + sky + ground, spread into a `b3d(...)` |
| `demoSun(opts)` | A sun that casts shadows, at the device's shadow budget |
| `patternGround(opts)` | A ground that RECEIVES shadows and shows the light |
| `orbitCam(el, opts)` | The standard orbit camera, tilt-clamped, in `sceneCreated` |
| `spinner(el, opts)` | A slowly-rotating textured box, so you can see shadows move |
| `flightStage(opts)` | A setting an **aircraft** can operate in — stage, library, and a death panel that respawns you |

## Angles are DEGREES

`orbitCam` takes `alphaDeg`/`betaDeg`, per the framework rule: a bare angle name
is already degrees, and radians appear only where the maths needs them. The
radian `alpha`/`beta` pair is deprecated; it is still accepted and converted.

## Textures

Helpers take a `texture` URL rather than exporting asset paths: a path like
`/tosi-warhol-testgrid.svg` resolves only on **this** site, not in your project.
Pass your own, or omit it for a generated checker that needs no asset at all.

# UI

<!--{ "order": 120 }-->

**One UI that renders twice.** Every control here is a `Widget3d`: it draws to
SVG and takes pointer input as *coordinates*, never as DOM events. That single
choice is what lets the same object be a flat overlay, a texture on a panel in
the scene, and something you poke with a controller in a headset — without a
second implementation, and so without the two drifting apart.

## Kitchen sink

Every family at once, flat and on a plane, bound to the same state. Type in the
field (the ⌨ glyph toggles the on-screen keyboard), drag the curve, pick a tool.

```js
import {
  b3d, b3dLight, panelScene, panel3d, label3d, slider3d, toggle3d, select3d,
  button3d, row3d, vector3d, curve3d, iconGrid3d, ui,
} from 'tosijs-3d'
import { elements } from 'tosijs'
const { div, pre } = elements

const out = pre({ style: { margin: '8px 16px', color: '#8ea', font: '12px ui-monospace,monospace' } }, '')
const state = {
  name: 'scout',
  speed: 40,
  lights: true,
  material: 'matte',
  pos: { x: 0, y: 1.8, z: -4 },
  tool: 'move',
}
const show = () => {
  out.textContent =
    `name ${state.name}   speed ${state.speed}   lights ${state.lights}\n` +
    `material ${state.material}   tool ${state.tool}\n` +
    `pos ${state.pos.x}, ${state.pos.y}, ${state.pos.z}`
}

// The field is near the TOP on purpose: the on-screen keyboard opens below it,
// and refuses if there is not room — so a field at the bottom of a panel shows
// an inert glyph.
const nameField = ui.inputField({ value: state.name, handleChange: (v) => { state.name = v; show() } })

const TOOLS = [
  { icon: 'move', label: 'move' },
  { icon: 'rotateCw', label: 'turn' },
  { icon: 'resize', label: 'scale' },
  { icon: 'trash', label: 'delete' },
]

const panel = panel3d(
  { width: 320, height: 460 },
  label3d({ text: 'Kitchen sink', bold: true }),
  label3d({ text: 'name — tap the ⌨ glyph', muted: true, compact: true }),
  nameField,
  slider3d({ label: 'speed', value: state.speed, min: 0, max: 100, showValue: 'always', handleChange: (v) => { state.speed = v; show() } }),
  toggle3d({ label: 'lights', value: state.lights, handleChange: (v) => { state.lights = v; show() } }),
  select3d({
    label: 'material',
    value: state.material,
    options: ['matte', 'gloss', 'metal', 'glass'],
    handleChange: (v) => { state.material = v; show() },
  }),
  label3d({ text: 'position', muted: true, compact: true }),
  vector3d({ value: state.pos, step: 0.25, scrub: 0.02, handleChange: (v) => { state.pos = v; show() } }),
  label3d({ text: 'tool', muted: true, compact: true }),
  iconGrid3d({
    items: TOOLS, mode: 'radio', selected: 0,
    handleSelect: ([i]) => { state.tool = TOOLS[i].label; show() },
  }),
  curve3d({ kind: 'profile', label: 'response curve', aspect: 0.4 }),
  row3d({},
    button3d({ label: 'Reset', handleClick: () => { state.speed = 40; show() } }),
    button3d({ label: 'Apply', handleClick: () => { state.tool = 'applied'; show() } })
  )
)
show()

const { plane, sceneCreated } = panelScene({ svg: panel, target: panel, width: 2.4, camera: { radius: 3.4 } })
const scene = b3d(
  { style: { flex: 1, minWidth: 0, borderRadius: 8, overflow: 'hidden' }, sceneCreated },
  b3dLight({ intensity: 1 }),
  plane
)

// The flat presentation's own popup layer: a positioned sibling ABOVE the panel,
// outside its <svg>, so a keyboard is not cropped by the panel it belongs to.
// `panelScene` adds the scene's layer (a plane) separately — a popup opens in
// both, because the panel is on screen twice.
const flatHost = div({ style: { flex: '0 0 320px', overflow: 'visible' } }, panel)

preview.append(
  div(
    { style: { display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', height: '100%' } },
    div(
      { style: { display: 'flex', gap: 20, flex: 1, minHeight: 0, padding: 14 } },
      flatHost,
      div({ style: { display: 'flex', flex: 1, minWidth: 0 } }, scene)
    ),
    out
  )
)
panel.useDomLayer(flatHost)
```
```css
.preview {
  height: 100%;
}
```

## The pieces

The pieces, roughly outermost first:

- **[widgets3d](/widgets3d/)** — the controls (`panel3d`, `slider3d`, `toggle3d`,
  `select3d`, `button3d`, `list3d`, `row3d`, `label3d`) and the `Widget3d`
  contract they all satisfy.
- **[box](/box/)** and **[surface](/surface/)** — the containers. A box wraps,
  scrolls and traverses; a surface adds an overlay layer for menus and panels.
- **[popup-surface](/popup-surface/)** — a popup is *another surface*, on its own
  plane. Depth replaces z-index, and tearing one off is re-parenting rather than
  new machinery.
- **Editors** — [vector-field](/vector-field/) (a coordinate on one row),
  [curve-field](/curve-field/) and [footprint-field](/footprint-field/) (author a
  terrain province), [icon-grid](/icon-grid/) (segmented select, tool palette and
  mode picker in one), [keyboard](/keyboard/), [table](/table/).
- **[w3d-theme](/w3d-theme/)** — the tokens everything reads, and
  [theme-editor](/theme-editor/) to push them around live.

The pure models underneath (layout maths, key layouts, text editing) are
documented on the page that uses them.

## Callbacks are named `handleX`

Every callback option in the UI is `handleX`: `handleChange`, `handleSelect`,
`handleActivate`, `handleClick`, `handleClose`, `handleKey`. The `onX` spelling is
not read, and passing one logs a warning once per name, naming the replacement. The
reason is the element creator: on a tosijs component it binds any `on*` prop as a DOM
event listener, so an `onChange` callback would never be called and nothing would
say so. `handleX` cannot be mistaken for an event name, and it works the same on every
widget. Components take `whenX` (`whenDestroyed`) or a verb (`drive`) for the same
reason. A widget of your own reads its callbacks the same way:
`handlerOf(config, 'handleChange', 'onChange')?.(value)`.

# 0.11.4

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9988996 }-->

## Added

- **A character creator, on MakeHuman's CC0 body** (CHARACTER-DESIGN.md). Try it on the [character builder](/character-builder/) page: a person walking while you reshape them. The data is a **human pack** on the CDN (`makehuman/hm08/`), loaded with `loadHumanPack`.
  - **Body**: `macroWeights` / `morphHuman` turn gender, age, muscle, weight, height, proportions and an ancestry mix into a body, in about a millisecond.
  - **Skeleton**: `humanRig` places UAL's 65 joints from the body's own joint cubes, and bone heat binds the skin once per base, so UAL's clips play on any body shape (`buildRig`, `retargetClip`). `humanBody` draws a body unrigged.
  - **Skin**: one dial from very fair to very dark through the Monk Skin Tone Scale, plus redness (`skinMaterial`, `skinAlbedo`); lips tinted from it over the pack's `lips` region, no UVs needed (`lipTint`, `lipAlbedo`).
  - **Eyes**: `humanFace` adds eyes and eyelashes that fit every body (they are the base mesh's own helper vertices); the iris is drawn in code with a colour dial (`eyeTexture`, `irisColor`); `eyeGaze` aims the eyes at a world point with small saccades.
  - **Hair**: Quaternius' CC0 hairstyles, beards and eyebrows, modelled for another head, fitted to any body (`loadHairLibrary`, `headScalp`, `humanHair`); tinted by `hairColor` (black to platinum, plus red). The pure fit is `fitToScalp` / `conformOutside`.

## Fixed

- **Retargeting no longer lines a character's collarbones up with the clip's.** A collarbone's rest direction is the body's shape, like the spine's; where two rigs differed (UAL's runs back to the shoulder, MakeHuman's lies flat), every clip shrugged the shoulders.

# 0.11.3

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9988997 }-->

## Added

- **`blendSeconds` on `<tosi-b3d-biped>`** (default 0.25): how long each animation change eases over. `0` cuts.
- The panel page's system-bar demo has a "New journal entry" button that blinks the Journal button (`attention()`).

## Changed

- **The biped eases every animation change** instead of cutting: walk to run, standing to crouch, the gun coming up and going down, aim up/level/down. The blend is timed, so it lasts the same at any frame rate. A crouch at rest plays a transition clip if the states name one (`sneakEnter` / `sneakExit`, e.g. UAL's `Crouch_Enter` / `Crouch_Exit`); the defaults have none, so it blends.
- **The sun's shadow bias defaults are now `shadowBias` 0.002 and `shadowNormalBias` 0.04**, which clears the fine acne stripes on plain lit surfaces. If a small caster's shadow detaches, set them lower on your `<tosi-b3d-sun>`.
- **In the biped mapping, clicking the right stick (R3) toggles the weapon**, as the right bumper does. The playground's glass pad shows both stick clicks.

## Fixed

- **XR thumbsticks have the hardware pad's 0.15 per-axis deadzone**, so a stick pushed sideways to turn no longer drifts the biped's look pitch (its aim). Raising the weapon now levels the aim in a headset too.
- In the glass gamepad demo, the cube moves away from you on left stick up, and the readout sits top centre, clear of the system bar.

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9988998 }-->

## Added

- **A new glass gamepad**, laid out like a pair of VR controllers held flat: on each side a trigger, bumper, stick and two face buttons (X and Y on the left, A and B on the right, in Xbox colours), with view and menu between them at the bottom. It is one SVG sheet (`static/glass-gamepad.svg`) that the pad cuts into three clusters along the bottom; on a narrow screen the centre cluster tucks in between the others when it fits and sits above them when it does not.

# 0.11.0

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9989000 }-->

**0.11 in one paragraph.** Any character plays the Universal Animation
Library: `retarget` reads which bone is which across UE, Mixamo, Kenney and
Blender names and transfers clips across A- and T-poses; a mesh with no
skeleton is auto-rigged from eight markers (`fitSkeleton`, fingers, mittens
and tails found from its shape, `boneHeat` binding, `buildRig`); hair and
tails hang on spring bones; the rig tool does it all in the browser and saves
a recipe (`applyRigRecipe`), and mounts in a host's scene (`mountRigTool`).
Effects are particles, light and sound as layers on one clock
(`<tosi-b3d-effect>`, presets from volcano to sparks, procedural sprites and
voices), edited in the effect tool (`mountEffectTool`). Around them:
`inspectView` (held orthographic views), `seamMaterial`, `barMenu`, slider
stops, landform schemas, the biped's sprint. Nothing was removed; see
Migration.md for the behaviours that changed. Size over the 0.10 line: see
the release's Size line.

## Added

- **System panels from code, and a button that asks to be looked at** (#3436, Manta's objectives list): `<tosi-b3d-panel>` has `show()`, `hide()`, `toggle()` and `isOpen`, and fires `paneltoggle` (`detail.open`) whenever it opens or closes, by code or by its button, so a list can put itself away after a while. `attention(ms?)` blinks its button on the system bar, flat and in a headset (and on the HTML lozenge with `flat-ui="dom"`). Before the scene is up, `show()` means open at start.
- **`systempanels` on `<tosi-b3d>`** (#3436): fires (bubbling) on every system panel opened or closed, with `detail.panel`, `detail.shown`, `detail.byUser` (opened by its button, not by code) and `detail.open` (every open one, `{ panel, byUser }`), so the game decides what it means: `e.detail.open.some((p) => p.byUser)` pauses while the person has one up. A headset session starting or ending is reported once, after it, with `panel` null. `paneltoggle` also carries `byUser`.

## Changed

- **The glass gamepad stands aside only for system panels the person opened** (#3436). One opened by its button hides the pad as before; one opened by code (`show()`, `open` at start) leaves it up, because it is up while they play and on a phone hiding the pad took the controls away. Give one that stays open a `screenAnchor` clear of the pad.

## Fixed

- **The effect tool's `listen from` works in a headset** (Tonio). Flat it pulls the camera back; in a headset you are the camera, so it did nothing. There the effect now moves along the ground, on the line from you to it, to that distance (on entering the session too, so the sound's lateness on the status line is true), and goes back when the session ends.
- **A tool's settings panel shows its changes in a headset** (Tonio, the rig tool in VR: picking a face stopped the clip, but the animate toggle still showed it on, so turning it off and on again was needed to play). `refreshScenePanel()` rebuilt only the flat panel; it now rebuilds the headset's too. The rig tool's doc says what `view` means in a headset (you are the camera: it switches between still and playing) and names the faces it takes.
- **The system bar keeps working after the glass pad** (Tonio, in a headset's flat browser: open and close the inventory, drag the pad's stick twice, and the bar stopped answering until a click elsewhere on the page). Babylon keeps one canvas slot per touch (`navigator.maxTouchPoints`, else 2) and gives a touch it sees move without a press a slot retroactively; when that touch was released on the pad (which captures its own pointer), the canvas never heard it, and with every slot held Babylon ignored new presses ("Max number of touches exceeded"). A touch or pen released anywhere off the canvas is now cancelled on the canvas too, which frees its slot.
- **Effect sounds stop when you leave** (Tonio, in the headset: leaving the effect tool page left its sound playing). A voice lives in the page's audio context, not the scene, and a scene that went away never stopped its voices, so they looped on. Now a disposed scene stops every effect voice it was playing, and the effect audio is suspended while the tab is hidden (a hidden tab draws no frames, so nothing would fade a voice out).
- **The pause panel says "Continue in VR" only where there is VR** (#3431, Manta): with `enterXrOnResume="on"` it said so on an iPhone and a laptop too, where resuming just continues. It now needs the headset helper as well, which is built only when `immersive-vr` is supported.
- **A biped's sprint ends when it stops** (0.11.0 gate): the sprint is held down to 70% of full speed so a trigger near the line does not flicker, but the flag was only updated while running forward, so a stop, swim or sidestep left it set and the next run went straight into the sprint at 75%. # 0.10.19

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9989981 }-->

## Added

- **Auto-rig finds the fingers a mesh has** (Tonio: the skinny weasel has three fingers and a thumb, and they were not rigged). Palm down in a T-pose, fingers are separate only from above, so `fitSkeleton` looks down on each hand (`MeshQuery.fromAbove()`): slices across the hand from the tips back find the fingers as separate runs, where they join is the knuckle, and a prong that reaches forward near the wrist is the thumb. Each joint sits along the real finger at the middle of its thickness, and found fingers take the skin (the hand then runs to the knuckles). `rig.fingers` says which were found; the rest are placed by proportion as before and take none. The skinny weasel gets index, middle, ring and thumb; omnidude's mitten an index and a thumb; the chunky weasel's paws none.
- **A strand is laid along a path** (Tonio: map out the tail or the ponytail, not one stub, and choose how many links). `StrandSpringRecipe.path` is the line it follows at rest, root first; its `segments` links are spaced evenly along it (`strandPoints`). In the rig tool every point is an orange handle you drag, `+ point` adds one beyond the tip, `− point` takes one away, `links` sets the count, and the chosen strand marks where each link falls. A straight strand still reads as before, and `setStrandPath` keeps `offset`, `length`, `yawDeg` and `pitchDeg` true to a path for a reader that knows nothing of paths.
- **The rig tool snaps its view** to a face of the character (see `inspectView` below), and its API gains `view` and `play(clip)`. A bone chain spring shows every link, not only its first bone, and an auto-rigged tail has a `tail links` slider.
- **`inspectView(camera)`: front, back, side, top and bottom views, orthographic and held** (Tonio, #3419). It turns an `ArcRotateCamera` orthographic and pins it to a face, so a drag no longer orbits and is free for what is under the pointer; pan and zoom still work. The camera's own `radius` is the zoom: each frame the orthographic box is what a perspective camera at that radius would show, so leaving the view leaves the scene the same size. The near plane moves behind the camera, so zooming in close never cuts the subject open.
- **Panels and the system bar work under an orthographic camera.** They were placed from the camera's field of view, so they shrank to a stamp. `viewSpanAt(camera, d, w, h)` in frame-panel answers both kinds of camera.
- **`barMenu(...)`: a system-bar button that is a menu**: one press opens a short list under the bar, a choice closes it, flat and in a headset. `viewMenu(inspect, scene, options)` is the camera one: it picks the face or `perspective`, and its faces, labels and whether it stays in the perspective view can all be configured.
- **`seamMaterial` / `withBarycentrics`: a mesh drawn as its polygons**: a flat fill (desaturated pink by default) with soft white edges, drawn in the fragment shader from barycentric coordinates, so the edges are smooth and the same width in pixels at any zoom; they fade where triangles shrink to a few pixels. `seamOverlay(mesh)` draws a twin in the mesh's place (its own unshared geometry, the same skeleton), so the mesh itself is untouched.
- **The rig tool's view is its pose** (Tonio): standing at rest it is orthographic (front by default) and drawn as its polygons; `perspective` plays the clip. The camera on the system bar picks either, and the animate toggle moves the view the other way. Seen from a side, the mannequin stands beside the character rather than in front of it.
- **Auto-rig: a hand with no fingers apart gets a mitten and a thumb** (Tonio, the space marine's claws). Seen from above such a hand is one blob, so no finger was found and four were placed by proportion, in the air past a claw that hooks down. Now its middle line is followed slice by slice from the wrist (the middle of the flesh in height and depth across each slice), so one chain (the index, as Mixamo's mittens have) runs down the hook to its tip. A thumb that grows straight out of the palm's edge, with no gap, is found as a bump on the palm's front edge. The chunky weasel's paws get a mitten each, so a paw curls on a grip.
- **The seam material hides the diagonals that split quads** (Tonio): `quadDiagonals` finds the quads again (two triangles sharing the longest edge of both, nearly flat together) and that edge is not drawn. `withBarycentrics(mesh, { quads: false })` draws every edge.
- **The biped sprints**: near full speed it plays the rig's `sprint` state (UAL's `Sprint_Loop`, already mapped by `ualAnimationStates()` but never played) instead of the jog sped up, held until the speed drops back a little so an analog trigger does not flicker between them. A rig without a sprint clip jogs as before (Tonio).
- **`inspectStage(scene)`**: a neutral floor to look at a model on (light grey, ruled every metre and faintly every quarter) and a key light. The rig tool stands on it. Shadows are not on yet (see #3420).
- **The rig tool's mannequin is a ghost** (translucent, so it compares without competing), and its toggle is called `mannequin` (it was `compare`). The glTF loader marks materials opaque, which `visibility` alone cannot override, so they are set to blend. The clip picker lists loops first.
- **The seam material can receive shadows**: `seamOverlay`'s twin receives them, and `shade` (now 0.45 by default) is the part of the fill that light, and so shadow, reaches. Fill and line colours are options.
- **The effect tool mounts in a host's scene** on the same contract (tosijs-3d#122, for ensemble's `effect` piece): `mountEffectTool(b3d, { recipe, target, files, stage, camera })`, `change` and `commit` with the recipe, a system panel when hosted, `unmount()` that returns every count. `effectTool()` is the same tool in a scene of its own.
- **A scene's last effect player takes the shared parts with it**: the per-scene driver observer, pooled lights and sprite textures are released when the last `EffectPlayer` in a scene is disposed (they used to stay until the scene went), and made again by the next effect.
- **The rig tool mounts in a host's scene** (tosijs-3d#122, for ensemble's `figure` piece): `mountRigTool(b3d, { models, recipe, files, stage, camera })` returns a handle firing `change` (every edit) and `commit` (one per finished gesture) with a copy of the recipe, its `api`, and `unmount()`. `files: false` drops save, load, copy and the browser's working copy; `stage: false` adds no floor or light; a given camera is driven and restored exactly (angles, distance, target, projection, limits). Hosted, its panel is a system panel. Unmount (safe twice, and mid-load) returns the scene's mesh, material, texture, node, skeleton, animation, observer and panel counts to where they were, checked headless. `rigTool()` is now the same tool mounted in a scene of its own, with `change` and `commit` dispatched on the element.

## Changed

- **A character's head is no longer tipped back by its own neck** (Tonio: the weasels looked up). Retargeting lined every bone up with the source's rest direction, which is right for a limb (an A-pose against a T-pose) and wrong for the body's axis: the weasel's neck leans forward to a chin under its snout, and pulled upright to match the mannequin's, it tipped the head up by about 14° through every clip. The hips, spine, chest, neck and head now take the clip's turn as it is.
- **A tap on the body no longer reassigns a bone on its own** in the rig tool (Tonio: on an iPhone the weasels' heads sank into their chests and a tail pointed forward). The chosen role starts as the head, and any press that did not travel set the head's bone to whatever was under it. On a phone that was every attempt to orbit, and the tool remembered it. Now a tap sets a bone only right after a dot, the role or `clicking sets` was chosen, and only once. `start over` clears a recipe that was already changed.
- **The weasels' tails are stiffer** in the rig tool (Tonio: too floppy): stiffness 0.6 and damping 0.85, down from 0.25 and 0.6, which cuts the tail tip's sway on a walk to about 40%. A recipe the tool remembered keeps its own values; `start over` takes the new ones. Stiffness is the knob for floppiness: damping only trims the swing a little.

It is now written only when `scale` (or the node) changes, and the attribute still wins whenever it is set.
- **Projected AO darkens library pieces** (#107, from ensemble): it hooked only the materials in `scene.materials` and those created after it started, but a library's instances share its container's materials, which are in neither. So pieces placed from a `<tosi-b3d-library>` were left out of the depth picture and never occluded, while the plugin count said AO was running. It now also finds materials through the scene's meshes, at start and as meshes are added. On twelve pirate-kit pieces, the pixels it changes went from 0% to 5.8% at strength 1, and from 0.1% to 16.5% at strength 3 (screen AO: 13%).
- **A key is delivered once even when a handler re-renders its field group mid-keystroke** (#94, from ensemble): a `handleChange` that rebuilt its panel inside the keydown detached the focused field's group, so the window listener, deciding afterwards, typed the key a second time (`flagXXship`). Every route now marks the event it consumed and skips one already marked.

It now needs the sun close behind (full within about 15°, gone by about 50°) and keeps its breadth. A first attempt that narrowed the band itself was rejected ("a very thin effect which isn't what I wanted"); Tonio, on this one: "pretty perfect".

A system draws a world a few units across, so the synthetic Earth read a fiftieth of one noise wave and came out as a single smooth landmass ("very Fisher Price Pangaea"). # 0.10.8

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9989992 }-->

## Added

- **`planetSchema()`** (`sceneSchemas.planet`): `<tosi-b3d-planet>` described like the other scene primitives, with sections (World, Surface, Sea, Air, Clouds, Craters, Rings, Gas giant, Maps), `heightMap`/`colorMap` marked as fetched, and the `world`/`gas` lists taken from the preset tables so they cannot drift. **`x-preset-written`** names the attributes a `world` preset writes into the planet. A consumer that applies schema defaults on bind should show them but not write them back over the preset (#103, ensemble).
- **`lat` / `lon` on `<tosi-b3d-terrain>`**: where this ground is on its planet, the latitude and longitude of the terrain's origin in degrees, so "this ground is at 12° N, 40° E" is one attribute pair, in markup and in `terrainSchema()`. `worldU`/`worldV` are now JS properties over them (`worldU = lon / 360`, `worldV = (lat + 90) / 180`). Before, they were plain properties that markup could not set and that needed a `regenerate()`. Changing `lat`/`lon` (or either view of them) rebuilds the ground. The defaults (-45, 0) are the old 0.25 / 0, so nothing moves (#103).
- **`seamBlend` / `seamWeight`** (`sphere-map`): make a layer laid out in flat metres periodic round a world, mixed with its copy one circumference away near the far meridian and untouched elsewhere.

## Fixed

- **A widget bound to a tosijs box lets go of it** (#100). `toggle3d`, `slider3d` and `select3d` subscribed to a bound box and threw the unsubscribe away. Every bound row left a listener in tosijs's module-level list that held the row, its panel and its host, so ensemble's editor grew by 125 listeners and 5,360 nodes per round of panel rebuilds. Each now unsubscribes in its `dispose()`. `B3d` already disposes the widget lists it rebuilds, and **`panel3d(…)` has a `dispose()`** that disposes its rows, for a consumer that drops its own panels. Not reaped by `isConnected`: an in-scene panel's SVG is never in the document.
- **Removing the last instance of a library model no longer turns every later one white** (#102). `disposeMeshTree` disposed a material when no mesh in the scene used it, but a library's source meshes live in its AssetContainer, out of that list, so the guard could not see that the library still needed the material. Ensemble's editor lost the colour of a whole kit on its first rebuild, and a game would see it when the last enemy of a type despawned and the next one spawned white. It now disposes only materials the scene owns (`scene.materials`); a container's are the container's.
- **A frozen or paused scene builds its system bar** (#3342). The bar and flat panels were built only on running frames, so a scene that started frozen (Manta freezes on every menu) showed the HTML lozenge, and a `<tosi-b3d-panel icon title>` got no button until it unfroze. Stopped frames keep the scene's chrome current now, as they already did its fog.
- **A sphere terrain joins at the far meridian** (#3318). Its noise is read on the sphere and always repeated; its profile fields (`blendProfiles`, `profileField`) and landforms (`craterField`, …) read flat metres and did not. The ground opposite the terrain's origin (longitude 180 at the default `worldU`) was two different places: a 116 m step on Manta's cratered moon, 19.5 m without the craters. Within 5% of a turn of that meridian they are now mixed with their copy one turn away, so the two sides meet. Elsewhere the ground is exactly as before, and a place one whole turn round is the same place. Spheres only: a cylinder is used as a big flat world with things placed in metres.
- **A globe of a world with no sea is drawn at its size** (#3319). A planet drawn from a `PlanetSurface` measured every height from `seaLevel`, so a dry world that says "no sea" with a sea level far below its ground (Manta's -10000 m) gained that depth as ground. A globe meant to be 40 units across came out at 2476. The globe now measures from the higher of the sea and the lowest ground. A world with a real sea is unchanged, and on a dry world the lowest ground sits on the base radius. The convention for "no sea" is a `seaLevel` below all of the ground.

One that is open when you enter or leave VR comes with you. Both come through `b3d.showModal(svg, height, fallback)`: where the scene has no modal to give (`flat-ui="dom"` on a monitor, a custom `setupXr` rig) it calls `fallback`, the caller's own presentation (the pause's DOM host, the respawn's world plane), including after entering or leaving VR, so a respawn panel never simply vanishes. - **Title bars: the title is centred, and the move and × glyphs are centred in the bar with the same margin at the side as at the top** (they were pulled into their corners). The × is drawn larger than the move glyph so the two read the same size: Feather's × covers 12 of its 24 units and the move arrows 20. The HTML panel centres its title too. This is all `chromeLayout`, so popups, `panel3d`, `titled3d` and the settings panel get it alike.
- **A focused frame panel no longer swells and shrinks with your head** in a headset: its fit to the view is worked out once per focus (and per content size), not every frame.

- **A sky with its own moons no longer draws Earth's.** At night the skybox drew its built-in moon on the replayed day arc and lit the scene from it, even when `<tosi-b3d-moon>`s gave the sky other moons: on Io (Land and Sky) a bright disc sat low in the east under Jupiter and read as the sun, while Jupiter was lit, correctly, by the real sun set in the west. Now a sky's own moons replace the built-in one, and the night light comes from the first of them, as bright as its sunlit face (Jupitershine).
- **A popup opened from the in-scene settings panel can be moved and closed, and fits the screen.** Its × and title bar were tested by a pick in the main scene, but it lives in the `ui` layer's own scene (which also keeps the press from the main scene's observers), so neither did anything; popups are now picked in their own scenes, layers first. A screen-pinned panel's popup is built no taller than the screen (a layer host's `roomFor`; it scrolls past that) and kept on it, where it used to hang from its row at up to 480 px and run off the bottom (the solar system's 27-body picker).

- The glass gamepad really steps aside for a menu: `suppress` hid it with `visibility`, which parts of the pad override, so bits of it still drew and took presses meant for the panel under it. It uses `display` now.
- Full screen: a scene removed and re-added no longer gets a second toggle on its button (one press went in and straight back out), and a refused request no longer throws an unhandled rejection.

It is solved with `anchorLayout` every frame and placed square to the screen in the head-locked frame, so a resize or a different window shape keeps it where you put it; it wins over `flatAnchor`'s degrees, which suit a headset, where a panel is around you. The demo loadouts use it: 64 px in, 2vmin down, 14% of the screen tall. Opened, a screen-pinned panel comes to the middle of the screen square to it, not tilted up from below eye level.
- **A box scrolls with a pointer alone**: a scrollbar on its right edge when its content overflows a fixed height (drag the thumb; press the track to page). A wheel scrolls a box on a page, but a panel in a scene gets no wheel and a headset has none, so a long list was cut off with no way to reach the rest. **Sticky children** (`sticky: true` on a leading run) stay put while the rest scrolls under them: the inventory list's heading and drop row (#3290).
- **The Biped Playground has the loadout, and the pistol lives on your hip.** Firing mode follows where the pistol is: in a hand the gun is up, on the hip it is down, in the bag or dropped there is nothing to raise. The weapon button draws it from the hip or holsters it, and dragging it into a hand does the same. `b3dBiped`'s new `whenWeapon` (JS) lets a game answer the weapon button itself and call `setGunplay`; `demoLoadout({ equip })` starts with things worn and returns its `inv` (#3305).
- **The Biped Playground has a pool**: 14 x 10 m, 3.5 m deep, in the far corner past the catwalk, with a shelving ramp at one end to walk in on (where `isSwimming`'s hysteresis is tested) and caustics on the floor. Sunk into the ground, because a biped swims anywhere below the water's height: `b3dGround`'s new `holes` (JS) cuts rectangles out of it, keeping its texture unbroken around them. `playground({ pool: false })` leaves it out.
- **A drop target.** `inventoryPanel`/`inventoryDock` `handleDrop(item, kind, from)` adds a **drop** row at the top of the list: a thing dropped there leaves the inventory, after the game has had its say (return reasons to refuse and it springs back; otherwise put it in the world). Both demos have one (#3290).
- **`ui.anchorLayout`, the third layout** beside the flow: positioned and layered. An item is pinned to any edge with an offset (units or a fraction, `'50%'`), with a natural or fixed size; between two pins its size is what they leave and a stated size is a minimum. Its anchor (`anchorX`/`anchorY`, `anchor: 'center'`; default the top left) is the point a pin places and the way a minimum that does not fit overflows. `within` pins it inside a rectangle of the container (a window in the artwork). Paint order is the order given or `z`. Pure and unit-tested; the box mode that uses it is next (#3309).
- **Things have pictures, and say what they are.** An item kind's `icon` (SVG markup) is drawn on its tile: beside the name in a list, alone and filling a socket, and as the ghost a drag carries. Pointing at a thing, or selecting it with a gamepad, shows an info floater (its name, `description`, mass and what it adds by default; `info` replaces that), drawn in the ghost's layer so nothing clips it. `carryTile` takes `icon` and `info`. The demos load one picture per kind from `/item-icons.json` (#3290).
- **A frame panel can come to you.** Content that dispatches `panelfocus` (`detail: { focus: true }`) on its SVG brings its panel front and centre (`focusAnchor`, default straight ahead and a little low), enlarged (`focusScale`, default 1.9, at 0.75 m) and always revealed; `focus: false` sends it back. A focused panel never sits inside the camera's near plane (it is pushed out and scaled to look the same size) and is never bigger than the view (it fits 92% of it, allowing for being off-centre), so a monitor shows all of it. `flatAnchor` places a panel somewhere else in the flat view (the shoulder is off a monitor's edge), and `<tosi-b3d-panel>` takes `svg`, `flatAnchor`, `focusAnchor` and `focusScale` as JS properties. A frame panel also grows with its SVG's viewBox now, so content that opens wider gets a wider plane. `inventoryDock` asks for focus as it opens, and the main `tosi-b3d` demo pins your loadout up and to the left (over the shoulder in VR, the top left flat): touch or click it and it comes front and centre with your bag (#3290).
- **An inventory in 3D: `inventoryDock`.** A loadout that lives on a plane in the scene, flat and in a headset. Closed, it is the schematic alone, small; a tap opens it, with the list beside it (a bag) to drag to and from, and a button closes it. Both are drawn in one SVG, so a drag between them is one plane with one ghost (`carryGhostLayer`). Without a `list` it opens to the schematic alone (a craft fitted from a carrier's stock). Demo: "In 3D" on the inventory-box page, where the loadout replaces the "Inventory" placeholder over your shoulder (top left flat) and a touch brings it front and centre (#3290).
- **A two-handed weapon shows in both hands**: `inventoryPanel`'s `alsoIn(item, kind, at)` names the other slots an item takes up, where it is drawn faded (and can be picked up from either). The game decides which; the panel only draws it (#3290).
- **Drag and drop, as a model and on a panel** (INVENTORY-DESIGN step 1). `createCarry` is picking up and putting down with nothing drawn: what is carried and from where, the target under the pointer, and its verdict as REASONS; drop is all or nothing; dragging and two taps are one model, and one carry spans every panel. `carryTile`, `carrySocket` and `carryPanel` draw it on a box: things with decorations (a status bar, a damaged or broken outline, a badge), sockets that light when the held thing would fit, dim when not and say why, and a ghost that follows the pointer. A drag goes from one panel to another (they share the carry), and letting go outside every panel puts the thing back.
- **An inventory model** (`createInventory`, INVENTORY-DESIGN step 2): pure, with the game's catalogue, rules, contributions and prices plugged in. Holders hold slots (a paper doll, hardpoints, mounts), lists (a bag, a stock) and grids (a hull of boxes). A move is checked against every rule on a copy and kept only if all pass, so it happens completely or not at all; it can swap, split a stack, take from the catalogue, or pay. `stage()` is a draft that may be incomplete (a cart, a barter, a design not yet committed); `totals` adds up what is fitted (and what its mount adds); `damage` crosses off a system's boxes. `craft` runs a recipe (inputs used up, tools required but kept, outputs made, one move) and `compile` turns a finished design into a new kind (a ship class, a learned spell, a forged sword). Tested against a party, a loadout, a starship design, a shop and a smithy.
- **`inventoryPanel`**: one holder of an inventory on a panel, with drag and drop wired to the model, so a socket lights, dims and explains with the game's own rules. Panels sharing an inventory and a carry are a party, a trade or (with `moveFor` adding a price) a shop.
- **Schematics**: `inventoryPanel({ schematics: { body: svgText } })` draws a container as art, and its slots go where the art's sockets are (`data-slot="…"`, or ids in a `Sockets` group; `readSchematic` reads one). Sockets on art draw nothing at rest, outline when what is held fits, darken when not, and name themselves and the reason on hover. Demos: equip a person, arm a Manta from a carrier's counted stock, and a shop (its goods left, yours right, the deal in the middle: one `move` that buys, sells and pays, or does none of it). Panels take `height` (a scrolling list), `only`/`hide` (split one holder across panels) and `refuse` (a view's own reasons), and show the holder's purse.
- **A schematic is drawn at the art's own scale**, cropped to what it draws and shrunk only when the panel is too narrow (`schematicFit`), so a socket designed 44 units square is a 44-unit target, not whatever the file's margins left of it.
- **The demo schematics are coloured by CSS variables** with defaults for a dark panel (`--schematic-body`, `--schematic-socket`, `--schematic-socket-edge`, `--schematic-label`): a host restyles them on the page, and a texture draws the defaults.
- **A box child can be placed** (`at: { x, y }`): over the flowed child before it, at that offset, taking no flow space and hit first. Sockets on a schematic are this.

## Changed

- **The closed loadout is a small picture**: no heading over it and no sockets drawn, only what is in them (all return when open), corners rounded well past the panel's own, 0.125 m wide (was 0.3; `focusScale` 4.56 keeps the opened size), and flat it sits nearer the top-left corner (18° up, was 10°), square to the screen. Frame panel anchors gain `flatOn` (parallel to the frame's view plane rather than turned to face the eye) and `tiltDeg` (tip it about its own horizontal axis without moving it) (#3290).
- **Inventory list rows are full width**, so a row is a button you can hit anywhere along it. **Swimming starts chest deep** (0.65 submerged, down to 0.5 to stand again; it was waist deep, 0.5 and 0.35), and a swimmer rides a little higher than the last change (12 cm of water above the head bone, was 20; treading unchanged) (#3290).
- **The opened dock's list is as tall as the loadout beside it** (it scrolls), not a fixed 540 that made the whole dock taller than its picture. `height` still sets it explicitly (#3290).
- **An inventory panel's heading sits over its schematic's top left** (title, totals, the container's name) instead of stacked above it, so the picture is larger, which matters most on the small pinned loadout. A panel whose first container is not a schematic keeps its heading above (#3290).
- **SVG panels are mipmapped** (`SvgTexture` `mipmaps`, default `true`: trilinear, anisotropic 4). A panel is nearly always drawn smaller than its texture (1024 px over ~300 px of a Quest 3's view at arm's length), and unfiltered its hairlines broke up and its text crawled; the small pinned loadout's socket outlines were visibly broken and now draw whole. Every in-scene panel, popup and HUD goes through it. Mip generation measured under 0.1 ms per repaint at 1024 px; it costs a third more texture memory. `mipmaps: false` for a texture always seen at about a texel per pixel.
- **An inventory panel on a page fits the space it is given** instead of being cropped (`fit`, default on): side by side they shrink in proportion, in a column it is no wider than the column, never taller than its container, never larger than drawn, always the same shape. Anything the page sets inline on the host wins (#3290).
- The default body panels are an inventory over the left shoulder and a **journal** over the right (both were "Inventory") (#3290).
- `panelScene`'s orbit camera stops at half its starting distance (`camera.minRadius`), so zooming cannot pass through the panel (#3290).
- **A planet's edge has a golden hour.** Where you see its air edge on and the sun is low over it, the air takes the colour left when its own is scattered out: Earth's goes gold, Mars's dusty air goes blue. The whole lit rim takes it together, by how far the sun has gone behind the planet from where you are: lit from the side, the rim (its "poles" included) stays the air's own colour. Face on, nothing changes (#3285).

## Fixed

- **In a headset, a screen-pinned panel is where its VR anchor says** (found by the release review). Checked in the emulated headset.
- **Two-tap works on a page** (found by the release review). The page examples cancelled the carry on every `pointerup`, and a tap pick-up happens ON a release, so it was put straight back. `carryOverlay` now cancels a drag let go over nothing itself, after the panels have had the release, and never a tap; the examples no longer add their own.
- **A press on a panel in the scene no longer also works the game's controls.** The biped reads mouse buttons (the left button is A, a jump), so every press on the playground's loadout made the hero jump, and with a weapon up could fire it. A frame panel now cancels the `pointerdown` it takes, which by the web's own rule stops the matching `mousedown`/`mouseup`; the scene's picking is pointer events and carries on.
- **A focused panel fits the view a looking-down camera actually has.** Its room was worked out from where it sits in its frame, which is level while a follow camera pitches down; it is now measured in the camera's own view.
- **Swimmers ride lower.** The water sat at the head bone (the base of the skull), which left a treader's shoulders and arms out and a swimmer's head, shoulders and back riding on top. It now sits 10 cm higher on a treader (at the jaw: the head out) and 20 cm on a swimmer (over the back: the head breaking).
- **Raising the weapon aims straight ahead.** The aim is the look pitch, which kept whatever it was left at (looking at the ground, the last dive), so the gun often came up pointing at your feet. `setGunplay(true)` levels it, flat only (in a headset the aim is the controller); lowering the weapon leaves the view alone.

The eye now sits along the head's own axes, 10 cm up the skull, rather than offset along the body's level facing (#3291).
- **Aiming down while swimming dives.** At the surface a swimmer's buoyancy (set so the swim pose floats on the waterline) lifted about as fast as a downward stroke sank, so pitching down with the right stick and swimming went nowhere, and up is capped at the surface by design: the stick seemed to do nothing either way. A stroke aimed down now takes the vertical from buoyancy in proportion to how steeply and how hard you swim (`diveBuoyancy`); let go and buoyancy surfaces you as before. Measured in the new pool: 1.3 m deeper in two seconds, where it was 0.3.

It is gone from every example.
- **No more fine bands over every lit surface.** `<tosi-b3d-sun>`'s `shadowBias` default is 0.0005 (was Babylon's 0.00005). With `shadowNormalBias` at 0.02, which has to stay low or thin limbs lose their shadow, plain scenes (the primitives and getting-started demos) were striped with shadow acne on the ground, the boxes and the spheres. A character's shadow is unchanged. The attribute table also said `shadowNormalBias` defaulted to 0.05; it is 0.02.
- **The checker ground is checkered.** `b3dGround({ texture: 'checker' })` drew one flat grey: the texture clamped at its edge instead of repeating, so every tile past the first was the edge colour. It repeats now, and is mipmapped so it does not shimmer toward the horizon. Its dark squares are 70% of the ground colour (they were a fixed grey barely darker than the default ground).
- **Getting started opens on a running scene**: the first scene is a live example, and below it the same scene as plain HTML markup, live too.
- **A star system keeps real time.** Every day, month and year is the real one, and a new `timeScale` attribute (simulated seconds per real second, default 3600: an hour a second, an Earth day in 24 seconds) says how fast it runs; both demos have a log **time** slider from real time to a year every ten seconds. Planets used to turn once in about 80 seconds against a 60-second year, so they looked still, and moons took longer to go round their planet than the planet took to go round the Sun. Now `SystemPlanetSpec.day` (Earth days, negative backwards) and `SystemBodySpec.period` (a moon's month in days, negative backwards) carry the truth for Sol (Venus and Uranus turn backwards, Triton goes round backwards); a generated moon gets Kepler's month for a true distance (`moonPeriod`), a generated rock an Earth day, a giant a Jupiter one. Orbits, months and days are angles of one clock (`spinAngle`), so they keep time together and stop together with `animate`.
- **Dragging on a frame panel no longer turns the camera.** Flat, the camera's own controls took the same pointer, so a drag across a panel orbited the view behind it. A press on a frame panel now holds the camera's controls until release (#3290).
- **A drag that leaves its panel at once still drags.** A press on a thing, then a pointer that was already over another panel by its next move (a controller ray moves in big steps; so does a fast flick), forgot the press and dragged nothing. Leaving a panel with a thing pressed now starts the drag. Found driving the loadout with an emulated controller (#3290).
- **A trigger press in VR always counts, whichever hand it is.** Babylon points with one controller, the first to connect, and a press on the other one only switched to it: the press was dropped, so the first press of a session (and any press after the headset swapped controllers) did nothing. Now the right hand points first, and a press on the hand that is not pointing switches to it and is delivered. It reads Babylon's private per-controller state; a Babylon upgrade that renames it brings back the dropped press rather than breaking anything (#3290).
- An inventory panel's totals line is always there, so the first thing worn no longer pushes the schematic down (#3290).
- **Dragging between inventory panels works with a finger or a headset's laser.** Both are captured by the element they press, so the moves and the release never reached another panel; `inventoryPanel` now lets the capture go as it arrives (a mouse was never captured, which is why it worked on a desktop). And on a page the ghost is drawn in one overlay above every panel (`carryOverlay(carry)`, with `carryPanel(…, { ghost: false })`), so it crosses from one panel to the next instead of being clipped by each. A panel on a 3D plane keeps its own ghost (#3290).

- **A thing can be dragged out of a socket** (it could only be dragged out of a list), and a thing in a list is itself a place to drop into that list, so a long, scrolled list takes a drop anywhere. A thing put back in a list joins a stack of its kind with room (a missile returned to the carrier is counted again); one drawn from a stack swaps with what a slot held.

A planet takes `seaShallow`/`seaDeep` for its sea's colour (Titan's methane). The colours are the biome chart's (a dry warm world is red, a dry cold one grey).

The planet demo has a world picker.

- **One mesh for land and sea.** A planet with a colour map, or without the
  biome shading, is now a single sphere drawn by one shader
  (`createPlanetSurfaceMaterial`): land above sea level, water below, told
  apart per pixel by height. The coast is a smooth line however coarse the
  mesh (it was wherever the ground poked through a sea sphere), the water is
  pale in the shallows and dark in the deep, and the sea has the sun's
  glint, broken into sparkle by fine wave texture. `seaGlint`, `seaIce`.
  On a real-map planet `flatSea="on"` now means "this world has a sea".
  With `biome="on"` the land is classified by the biome shader itself: the
  plugin's own code runs inside the planet material, so it is the same
  chart, palettes, parameters and volcanism as terrain, and
  `planet.biomePlugin.params` is live as before. Every planet that is not a
  gas giant is drawn this way now; the translucent sea sphere is gone.
  What is steep is decided from the heights alone (the slope the biome
  shader reads is taken from the height field per pixel, not from the
  mesh's normals), so the sea bed has slopes too. Changing `ocean` or

  element, so a control bound to it survives a rebuild.

- **Crinkly coastlines on a procedural planet.** The mesh cannot hold a
  coast that turns tighter than about two of its cells, so the octaves of
  detail it cannot carry are added per pixel, to the height that decides
  where the sea ends, how deep it is and how high the land is. They follow
  `detailScale` and `detailAmplitude`: turn those up and the coast breaks
  into inlets and islands. Slope still comes from the mesh's heights.
- **Lakes glint.** `inlandWater="on"` on a planet with a `colorMap` guesses
  inland water from the picture (blue, or the near-black NASA's Blue Marble
  paints deep lakes) and gives it the sea's glint. The height map only knows
  the sea. The real-worlds Earth has it on, and that demo gained `clouds`,

# 0.10.0

<!--{ "parent": "CHANGELOG", "order": 9990000 }-->

**A quality release: the deprecated names are gone, and a long list of bugs
with them.** No new elements; what was added is tooling for measuring and
debugging on a device, and some defaults changed (listed under **Changed
defaults** below). Most of what breaks was announced in 0.8 and
0.9; three things were not, and are listed below with the rest:
`new MersenneTwister()` without a seed, `WorldStore` queries returning copies,
and `surface.openPanel`'s `onClose`. [Migration.md](https://3d.tosijs.net/Migration/) has every
pair and what to do.
